content: The Lana'i Hookbill, scientifically named Dysmorodrepanis munroi, was a species of finch belonging to the family Fringillidae. This bird was endemic to the island of Lana'i in Hawaii, meaning it was found nowhere else in the world. The species was last observed in the Kaiholena Valley and the Waiakeakua area of the island. Its extinction is attributed to habitat loss, primarily due to the conversion of native forests into agricultural land, such as pineapple plantations. The only known specimen of the Lana'i Hookbill was collected by G.C. Munro on February 22, 1913, in the Kaiholena Valley. This specimen is currently preserved in the Bishop Museum in Honolulu, Hawaii. No additional specimens have been collected or observed since that time. Munro himself reported two additional sightings of the bird: one on March 16, 1916, in the Kaiholena Valley, and another on August 12, 1918, in the Waiakeakua area. The 1918 sighting was the last confirmed observation of the species. Adult Lana'i Hookbills were described as having light gray plumage with a greenish tinge. Their underparts were paler, almost white in color. A light band was visible along the wings, and a distinct light marking was present above the eye. The bird's most unique feature was its bill: the mandibles curved towards each other, leaving a gap in the middle, with only the tip of the lower mandible making contact with the upper mandible. The total length of the bird was approximately six inches. The Lana'i Hookbill was an extremely rare bird, with only a few sightings ever recorded, all occurring between approximately 1912 and 1918. Some naturalists have speculated that the bird might have been a deformed individual of another species, given the scarcity of observations and the fact that only three individuals were ever reported. There was also debate about whether it was the same species as the O‘u (Psittirostra psittacea), another Hawaiian finch. However, a study conducted by James et al. in 1989 confirmed that the Lana'i Hookbill was indeed a distinct species. The bird's diet remains largely unknown, as it was never observed feeding in the wild. However, dissection of the stomach of the collected specimen revealed that it had consumed native berries from the island. Based on the unique structure of its bill and its relatively weak jaw muscles, some researchers have hypothesized that the Lana'i Hookbill may have fed on endemic land snails. If this was the case, the extinction of these snails due to human activities likely contributed to the bird's decline and eventual extinction. By 1918, much of the native akoko forest on Lana'i, which was the bird's natural habitat, had been destroyed and replaced by pineapple plantations. This significant habitat loss, combined with other factors such as the potential loss of its food sources, led to the extinction of the Lana'i Hookbill. The species was officially listed as extinct on the IUCN Red List in 1996. Nearly all information about this bird comes from Munro's observations and his book, The Birds of Hawaii (1960).
